newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-LEHMAN HOPES TO CASH-IN AS FRONTRUNNER AT U.S. OPEN.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-LEHMAN HOPES TO CASH-IN AS FRONTRUNNER AT U.S. OPEN.

text.p: Tom Lehman hopes to finally cash in as a frontrunner on Sunday as he carries a two-shot lead into the final round of the arduous U.S. Open at Congressional Country Club.

Lehman emerged with the third-round lead by posting a pair of birdies in the five holes he had to finish early on Sunday morning after Saturday's round was stalled by a two-hour delay due to a thunderstorm.
Lehman has been in the lead heading into the final rounds of the last two U.S. Opens, but finished third at Shinnecock Hills in 1995 and tied for second last year at Oakland Hills.
"Maybe three times is the charm," Lehman said. "The pressure is an added factor, but if you are strong enough mentally you can use it as an advantage. The thing is not to beat myself mentally."
The reigning British Open champion stood at five under par for the championship after completing his round of two-under 68 to jump over Jeff Maggert on the leaderboard.
"They're the best five holes I played all tournament. I hit every shot the way I wanted to. I've very excited about the way I played."

Maggert held a one-shot lead overnight at four under par but he bogeyed the 17th to slip back to three-under, where he was tied with 1994 Open champion Ernie Els, who ran off three birdies in the early morning to surge into contention.
"It was good to get the third round over and start looking forward to this afternoon," Maggert said.
"I spent a lot of time thinking about what I was going to do this morning over the night. I didn't get a lot of sleep."
Alone in fourth place was Colin Montgomerie of Britain, who finished up a 67 by going bogey-birdie on the two holes he had to finish to stand at two under par.

Montgomerie, who fired a brilliant 65 to lead the opening round before soaring to six-over 76 in the lightning-interrupted second round, warned that scoring could be very difficult for the last 18 holes.
"The greens are so fast now, so severe," the Briton said. "They've rolled them and rolled them, and cut them and I feel fortunate to have taken only seven shots on the two holes."
Els was relieved to have made his late charge.
"Tom is playing so solid," said the broad-shouldered South African. "To be too far away from Tom is not a good thing going into the final 18 holes."
